item.title: AppFlowy
item.description:
AppFlowy is positioned as an open-source alternative to Notion. It offers documents, kanban boards, grids, calendars, and linked databases in a single workspace, and the clients are built with Flutter and Rust for desktop and mobile. You can use the cloud service or host your own server, so notes can stay on hardware you control.

Privacy and ownership are the main selling points. Data is stored locally first, the code is open for review, and teams can modify it. The AI assistant can summarize, rewrite, and answer questions about your pages, and it supports local models through tools like Ollama for people who do not want content leaving their machine.

item.title: Box AI
item.description:
Box is a content management platform, and Box AI brings intelligence to the files stored there. Users can ask questions about a document, compare several files, summarize a long report, or generate text based on content in a folder. The answers come from the files themselves, so they can be traced back to a source.

For businesses, a strong feature is structured data extraction. Box AI can pull fields from invoices, contracts, and forms, such as dates, parties, and amounts, and put them in metadata that others can search and filter. Box AI Agents can be configured for particular workflows, and the platform lets admins choose among models from various providers.

item.title: Dia
item.description:
Dia puts an AI assistant at the center of web browsing. The address bar accepts both web addresses and questions, so you can search, ask about the page you are viewing, or have the assistant work across several open tabs, such as comparing products or summarizing a set of articles. It can draft writing in context and pull from what you have open.

The browser keeps familiar elements such as tabs and extensions, but adds features that use browsing history and open pages as context, with options for custom skills that package repeated prompts. It focuses on helping with everyday tasks like research, email drafts, and shopping comparisons.

item.title: Elasticsearch
item.description: Elasticsearch stores documents as JSON and indexes them so searches come back in milliseconds, even across billions of records. It began as a full-text search engine for things like product catalogs and website search, and it is also used heavily for logs, metrics, and security data. It is the core of the Elastic Stack, which adds Kibana for dashboards, and ingestion tools for getting data in. Companies use it wherever they need to search or aggregate a large volume of text-heavy data quickly.

item.title: Meilisearch
item.description:
Meilisearch focuses on delivering relevant results quickly with little configuration. Developers send their documents to it through a simple API, and it returns ranked results as the user types, with typo tolerance, synonyms, filtering, and sorting working out of the box. That makes it popular for adding search to a store or a knowledge base.

Newer features address AI. Hybrid search combines keyword matching with vector similarity, so a query can find results by meaning as well as exact words, and it can connect to embedding models. Teams can host Meilisearch themselves, since it is open source, or use the company’s managed cloud.

item.title: Typesense
item.description:
Typesense is built for instant search experiences, like the results that appear as a user types in a store or documentation site. It keeps its index in memory for speed, handles typos by default, and supports filtering, faceting, sorting, and grouping. Its API is simple, and client libraries exist for popular languages.

It also supports modern retrieval needs. Vector search lets applications find results by meaning using embeddings, and hybrid search combines that with keyword matching. Built-in features can generate embeddings, and a conversational search mode answers questions using retrieved documents. Developers can run Typesense on their own servers or use Typesense Cloud.

item.title: Almanac
item.description:
Almanac builds memory for an AI agent. Once you connect work accounts, it reads messages, calendar events, documents, and code activity and compiles what it learns into a wiki covering people, projects, and decisions. The wiki updates as new information arrives, so the agent does not start from zero each time.

The agent then uses that knowledge to do work. Teammates can send requests through tools such as Slack, and it checks the wiki for context before acting, which aims to reduce the repeated explaining that other assistants need. Connections can be personal or shared, so a company can decide how much of its information the agent sees.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: Submit AI Tools
item.description:
Submit AI Tools collects AI products in a searchable list. Visitors browse by category, read short descriptions, and click through to the tools. Makers submit listings to get discovered.

As with other directories, coverage depends on submissions and editorial review, so details can be incomplete or out of date. It works best as one of several places to scan.

The site is free. Check each tool’s own site for pricing and privacy information. Similar resources include Futurepedia, There’s An AI For That, Aixploria, OpenTools, and Best of AI. Submit AI Tools suits people browsing for AI products.

item.title: Bloomfire
item.description:
Bloomfire is a knowledge management platform. Employees add articles, files, videos, and Q&A to a central library, tag them, and find them later with search. The platform is meant to hold what a company knows so that people do not keep asking colleagues the same questions.

AI features make retrieval easier. Users ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from the company’s own content with links to sources, and the system can suggest related material and flag content that needs updating. Analytics show what people search for and where gaps exist.

item.title: Perplexity Pro
item.description:
Perplexity is an answer engine that searches the web and writes cited responses. The Pro tier raises limits on advanced searches and lets users choose among models, including Perplexity’s own and leading models from other labs, for harder questions.

Pro adds tools for research: upload and analyze documents, longer and more detailed searches, image generation, and access to deeper research modes that produce reports. Spaces let users organize topics and collaborate, and an API credit is sometimes included.

item.title: Andi
item.description:
Andi is a search engine for people who find link lists cluttered. You ask a question, and it returns a short answer with cited sources, plus links you can open. The idea is to combine the answering ability of a language model with the freshness of the web.

Privacy and design are part of the pitch. Andi has said it does not rely on advertising or sell user data, and the interface is clean, with options to refine a query and explore related questions. It is one of several startups, along with Perplexity, You.com, and Phind, that took on the conventional search model.

item.title: AnythingLLM
item.description:
AnythingLLM gives you a private place to talk to your files. You add documents, web pages, or other content to a workspace, and the app indexes them in a vector database. When you ask a question, it retrieves relevant passages and sends them to a language model, which answers with references.

Flexibility is the main draw. You can choose a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, or a cloud model from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and swap them without rebuilding your workspace. It has agents that can browse the web or run tools, supports multiple users and permissions in the server version, and offers an API and embeddable chat widget.

item.title: Anytype
item.description:
Anytype is a workspace for notes and structured information built around privacy. Data is stored locally and encrypted, and syncs between devices peer to peer or through backup nodes, so you keep ownership of your content rather than leaving it on a company server. The app is open source.

Its model uses objects and types. Everything is an object, such as a page, a person, a book, or a task, and each type has fields. Objects link to each other and appear in sets and collections, which function like databases. This lets users create a personal wiki or a custom organizer without code. Optional AI features can summarize and help write.

item.title: Arc Browser
item.description: Arc reimagined the browser. Instead of a row of tabs across the top, it uses a vertical sidebar where tabs are grouped into spaces, such as work and personal, each with its own pinned items and theme. Tabs that you do not use are archived automatically, and features like split view, boosts for customizing websites, and easels for collecting ideas made it a favorite of power users and designers. It is built on Chromium, so most Chrome extensions work.

item.title: Bing Chat
item.description: Bing Chat was Microsoft’s first big move into AI-assisted search. It put a conversational assistant next to the Bing search box, so you could ask a question and get a written answer with links to sources instead of scanning a page of results. Microsoft later renamed and expanded it as Copilot, and the assistant now works across the web, in the Edge browser, in Windows, and in standalone mobile and desktop apps.

item.title: Devv.ai
item.description: Devv.ai was built as a search tool for programmers, positioned between a traditional search engine and a chatbot. You ask a technical question, such as how to configure a library or why an error occurs, and it searches documentation, GitHub repositories, and developer discussions and then writes an answer with sources. Linking to sources helps you verify the answer, which matters because chatbots can invent APIs or settings that do not exist.

item.title: Exa AI
item.description: Exa, formerly Metaphor, rethinks search for machines instead of people. Where a traditional engine matches keywords, Exa uses neural embeddings to find pages that are semantically similar to a query, even when they do not share words. You can search with natural-language descriptions, such as a list of startups building a specific kind of robot, and it returns results that match the idea. It can also take a link and find similar pages.

item.title: Glean
item.description:
Glean addresses the problem that company knowledge lives in dozens of separate tools. It connects to those systems through hundreds of connectors, builds an index of documents, messages, tickets, and other content, and lets employees search across everything from one box. Crucially, it mirrors the permissions of the source systems, so a person only sees results they would already have access to.

On top of search, Glean provides an AI assistant that answers questions in natural language using company information, with citations to the underlying sources. Employees ask things like how a process works, what was decided in a project, or what the latest customer feedback says, and receive a synthesized answer. Glean Agents let teams build automations and agents that take actions in connected apps, and a builder allows non-engineers to create them. Companies can choose among language models from several providers.

item.title: Kagi
item.description:
Kagi takes a different business model from other search engines: users pay a subscription, and in return there are no ads, no tracking-based profiles, and no incentive to favor advertisers. Results are meant to be clean and relevant, and the company says it does not sell data. The service uses several sources, including its own index of smaller sites, and puts effort into reducing low-quality content and SEO spam.

Control is a defining feature. Users can raise, lower, or block domains, so a site that is always useless for you disappears, and lenses restrict a search to a set of sources, such as forums or academic sites. AI tools include summaries of pages and videos, answers with citations, and an assistant that gives access to multiple language models. Kagi has also launched Orion, a privacy-focused browser, and other products around the search experience.

item.title: Liner
item.description:
Liner started as a tool for highlighting text on web pages and saving it. Users mark passages in articles and PDFs, which are collected and organized, so they can find them later. A browser extension and app make highlighting part of normal browsing.

AI features add search and summaries. An AI search engine returns answers with sources and surfaces relevant parts of highlighted content, and tools summarize pages and documents. A chat assistant answers questions about what a user is reading. It is popular with students and researchers, particularly in Korea where the company began.

item.title: Perplexity AI
item.description:
Perplexity positions itself as an alternative to the list of links. You ask a question in natural language, it searches the web in real time, reads the pages, and writes a concise answer with citations to each source. That format is helpful for questions where you want a quick overview with a way to check the evidence, such as product comparisons, news, how-to questions, and research basics.

The experience supports continued exploration. Follow-up questions build on earlier context, and focus options narrow the search to categories such as academic sources or discussion forums. Pro Search runs more steps for complex questions, and Deep Research generates longer reports. The Comet browser brings the assistant into everyday browsing, and Spaces organize related research. Users can choose among several models in paid plans.

item.title: Phind
item.description: Phind was built for programmers who had questions that a standard search engine handled poorly. A developer could ask how to fix an error, compare libraries, or write a function, and Phind searched the web and documentation, then wrote an answer with code snippets and links to its sources. It used its own coding-focused models and later offered an IDE extension and a chat interface for follow-up questions, and it was popular as a free alternative to general chatbots.

item.title: Readwise Reader
item.description:
Reader is a single inbox for things you want to read. You can save web pages, subscribe to newsletters at a dedicated email address, follow RSS feeds, upload PDFs and ebooks, and import videos with transcripts. Everything appears in a clean reading view, with tools for highlighting, tagging, and taking notes, and it works across web, mobile, and browser extensions.

The connection with Readwise makes it more than a reading list. Highlights flow into Readwise, which resurfaces them through spaced repetition so you remember what you read, and exports them to Notion, Obsidian, Roam, and other note apps. Ghostreader is the AI assistant that can summarize a document, define terms, answer questions about it, and generate custom prompts, and it also supports text-to-speech and features for catching up on a backlog.

item.title: You.com
item.description:
You.com is a search engine that mixes web results with AI-generated answers. You ask a question and receive a conversational response with links to sources, along with traditional results and apps for tasks like coding or image creation. A privacy focus has been part of its positioning, with a private mode and a commitment to not selling personal data.

The product has moved toward agents and enterprise search. Research and agent modes run multi-step investigations and produce longer reports, a custom agent builder lets people create assistants for specific tasks, and the platform lets users switch among models from different providers. For developers and businesses, You.com offers APIs that deliver live web search results formatted for AI applications, which several AI companies use to ground their answers.

item.title: Document360
item.description:
Document360 helps companies maintain help centers and internal documentation. Writers use an editor with categories, versioning, and review workflows, then publish to a branded site that customers or employees can search. Analytics show what people look for and which articles fall short.

AI makes content easier to find and keep up to date. Semantic search finds answers by meaning, a chatbot answers questions from the documentation, and suggestions point out gaps and outdated articles. Writers can also use AI to draft and improve content. Integrations connect with helpdesk and chat tools.

item.title: Guru
item.description:
Guru stores verified knowledge in cards that teams can find where they work. A browser extension and Slack integration surface relevant answers without leaving the page, and experts verify cards on a schedule so that the information stays trustworthy. The idea is a single source of truth for sales, support, and internal teams.

AI search connects to the company’s other sources, such as documents, chat, and ticketing systems, and answers questions in natural language with citations. Analytics show what people search for and which content is stale. Admins control who can see what, and the AI respects those permissions.

item.title: Slab
item.description:
Slab gives teams a clean place to write and organize internal documentation. Content is arranged in topics, and the editor emphasizes readability. Engineering, support, and operations teams use it for runbooks, handbooks, and policies.

Search is the core feature. It queries Slab content and connected tools such as Google Drive, GitHub, and Slack in one place, and the AI answers questions in natural language with links to sources. Verification features prompt owners to keep pages up to date.

item.title: Tettra
item.description:
Tettra helps teams keep answers in one place. Teams write pages for policies, processes, and FAQs, organize them in categories, and assign owners who verify content periodically so it stays accurate. Integrations with Slack make answers available where people ask questions.

An AI assistant searches the wiki and connected sources to respond to questions in chat. Requests that cannot be answered become tasks for subject experts, which grows the knowledge base over time.

item.title: Capacities
item.description: Capacities rethinks how a notes app is structured. Instead of one kind of page, everything you capture is an object with a type, such as a book, a person, a meeting, an article, or a project, and each type can have its own properties and template. You link objects together, so a book can connect to the people who recommended it and the ideas it inspired. The result is a graph of your knowledge that is easier to browse than a pile of untitled notes.

item.title: Logseq
item.description: Logseq is built on the idea that notes should be a network of connected blocks. You write in an outliner where each bullet is a block, link to other pages with double brackets, and see backlinks that show everywhere an idea is referenced. Daily journals are the default entry point, so you capture thoughts as they come and organize them through links instead of folders. A graph view shows how pages relate.

item.title: Mem
item.description:
Mem is built on the idea that notes should organize themselves. Users capture thoughts, meeting notes, and links without choosing folders, and the system connects related items and surfaces them when relevant. Search understands meaning, so finding an old idea does not require remembering exact words.

AI features extend this. A chat assistant answers questions using your notes, summarizes meetings, and drafts text from your own material. Integrations bring in content from calendars and other apps, so context accumulates in one place.

item.title: Notion AI
item.description: Notion is a workspace for notes, documents, wikis, and databases, and Notion AI works inside it instead of in a separate chat window. Highlight a paragraph and ask it to tighten the writing, summarize a long page, translate a section, or turn rough notes into a clean doc. It can also fill in database properties, such as tagging each row with a category or pulling action items out of meeting notes, which saves a lot of manual cleanup in busy workspaces.

item.title: Obsidian AI
item.description:
Obsidian’s approach to AI follows its general philosophy: keep the core simple and let users choose add-ons. Because notes are plain files in a folder, they work well with language models. Community plugins let you chat with your vault, ask questions about your notes, summarize long documents, rewrite text, and find related notes by meaning instead of keywords. Smart Connections and Copilot-style plugins are popular examples.

Users have a lot of freedom over where the AI runs. A plugin can send text to a hosted model like those from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google using your own API key, or it can connect to a local model through tools such as Ollama or LM Studio, so notes never leave your computer. Some people also expose their vault to coding agents and assistants through the Model Context Protocol, which lets tools like Claude read and organize notes.

item.title: Recall
item.description:
Recall acts as a personal archive that organizes itself. A user saves a web page, YouTube video, podcast, or document with a browser extension or app, and Recall produces a summary, extracts key points, and links the item to related content already in the library through a knowledge graph.

An assistant lets users ask questions across everything they have saved, and spaced repetition quizzes help them remember material. It suits people who consume a lot of information and lose track of it.

item.title: Reflect
item.description:
Reflect aims to be a quick place to capture thoughts and connect them. You write notes, link them to each other with simple syntax, and see backlinks that show where an idea is referenced. Daily notes serve as an inbox, a calendar view ties notes to meetings, and a graph helps visualize connections. The app is built for speed and a clean interface, with sync across devices.

The AI assistant works on your notes. It can summarize a page, rewrite text, brainstorm, and answer questions based on the content you have saved, and voice transcription turns spoken notes into text. Reflect also emphasizes privacy: notes are end-to-end encrypted, which limits what the company can see. Browser extensions and integrations let you save web content and connect with services like Kindle highlights and Readwise.

item.title: remio
item.description:
remio collects what you read and write in one place and lets you ask questions about it. It indexes notes, files, and web pages visited, then answers queries such as where an idea came from or what a document said, with links to the source.

The idea is to address the problem of forgetting where information lives. Capture happens automatically through a browser extension and app, with less manual filing than a traditional note tool.
